generation.hypothesis: A data‐driven machine learning model that integrates oxidation kinetics, microstructural, and compositional data can predict optimized processing conditions—such as stationary friction processing at high rotational speeds—that generate an ultrafine grain microstructure, thereby promoting the formation of dense and protective oxide scales (e.g., Cr2O3 and Al2O3) to enhance oxidation resistance in susceptible alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: Oxidation-prone metallic or high-entropy alloy surfaces (e.g., as-cast AlCoCrFeNi alloy) with a coarse grain structure obtained by conventional processing.
generation.intervention: Develop and apply a machine learning model trained on experimental datasets (including oxidation kinetics, microstructural metrics, and compositional information) to identify processing modifications, such as stationary friction processing at specific rotational speeds, that induce ultrafine grain structures.
generation.conditions: Exposure to high-temperature oxidizing environments (e.g., 850–1050 °C) where oxygen diffusion promotes oxide growth.
generation.structural_mediator: The creation of an ultrafine grain microstructure with increased grain boundary density that facilitates the rapid nucleation and growth of a continuous, passivating oxide scale (such as Cr2O3 and Al2O3).
generation.mechanism: Processing modifications identified by the machine learning model refine the grain size, which increases the number of grain boundaries. This microstructural refinement enhances the nucleation of protective oxides, thereby forming a dense oxide scale that acts as a diffusion barrier, reducing further oxidation.
generation.predicted_outcome: A significant reduction in oxidation kinetics (e.g., a 12–48% decrease in weight gain over time) compared to alloys processed with conventional routes.
generation.baseline: Alloys processed through conventional methods that exhibit coarser grains and less uniform oxide layers, leading to higher oxidation rates.
generation.boundary: The predictive accuracy of the machine learning model is likely limited to the range of experimental conditions and alloy compositions included in its training dataset; extrapolation to novel compositions or more extreme conditions may introduce uncertainties.
generation.uncertainty: While existing evidence supports improvements in oxidation resistance through grain refinement via stationary friction processing, it remains uncertain how universally the model’s predictions will translate across different alloy systems and processing regimes not represented in the training data.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples of an oxidation-prone alloy: one set processed by conventional methods and another set processed using the model-guided optimized conditions (e.g., stationary friction processing at high rotational speeds). Expose both sets of samples to high-temperature oxidizing conditions (850–1050 °C) for identical durations.
measurements: Weight gain measurements over time to assess oxidation kinetics
Microstructural analysis (SEM/TEM) to verify grain size refinement and grain boundary density
Phase analysis (e.g., via XRD) to determine the formation and continuity of protective oxide scales
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the model-guided processing does not yield a statistically significant decrease in oxidation kinetics (i.e., similar weight gain and oxide scale quality) compared to the conventionally processed samples, then the hypothesis that a data-driven approach can predict and optimize oxidation resistance is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract This work investigates the effect of ultrafine-grain microstructure on the oxidation behavior of AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy (HEA). The ultrafine-grain microstructure is obtained using stationary friction processing performed at two different rotational speeds, 400 and 1800 rpm, for 5 min duration. Processed samples demonstrate high depth of refinement (DOR) and ultrafine grain size (0.43–1 μm) at high rotational speeds along with significant phase transformations from BCC/B2 to FCC microstructure. Further, surface free energy of the ultrafine-grain microstructure is enhanced up to 35%. Oxidation kinetics of the ultrafine-grained sample is decelerated up to 12–48% in a temperature range of 850–1050 °C for a duration of 100 h. Chromia and alumina were the predominant oxides formed in almost all the samples oxidized at elevated temperature. In addition, spinel Co(Cr,Fe) 2 O 4 /Fe(Co,Cr) 2 O 4 formation is also detected in the unprocessed oxidized samples. Processed samples rich in grain boundaries (GBs) promote internal oxidation to form Al-rich inner oxides. A coarse grain microstructure having BCC/B2 phases was obtained in the as-cast HEA sample. Only 5 min of straining of sample significantly refined the grain structure from 98 to 1 μm and 0.43 μm for the SFP_400 and SFP_1800 sample, respectively. The ultrafine-grained samples showed a phase transition from BCC/B2 to FCC structure. The SFP_400 sample showed a 12–20% reduction in the oxidation kinetics, whereas the SFP_1800 sample showed a 38–48% reduction in the oxidation kinetics compared to the as-cast alloy. Low values of parabolic rate constant and high values of activation energy for the ultrafine-grained samples show the high oxidation resistance of the processed samples. Protective oxide scales of Al 2 O 3 and Cr 2 O 3 were predominantly found after discontinuous isothermal oxidation. Other than protective scales, the availability of Co(Cr,Fe) 2 O 4 spinel phases was also observed during the oxidation at elevated temperatures. The presence of more GBs favoring outward flux of elements to form a dense chromia layer followed by internal Al-rich oxide layered structure is responsible for the enhanced oxidation resistance of the processed samples.

decision.trend: Early studies in the field focused on experimentally assessing oxidation behavior in various high-entropy and refractory alloys under different temperature regimes. Researchers used conventional processing methods (e.g., arc melting, spark plasma sintering, and laser cladding) and tested the kinetics and mechanisms of oxide scale formation, emphasizing how microstructure, grain size, and phase formation influence the development of protective oxides (such as Cr2O3 and Al2O3) versus nonprotective scales. More recent work has introduced processing techniques like stationary friction processing to promote ultrafine grain structures, which facilitate rapid formation of a dense, passivating oxide film. Although these studies have helped identify key processing parameters that govern oxidation resistance, the complexity and interplay of kinetic parameters, microstructural evolution, and alloying effects remain challenging to predict reliably.
decision.unsolved: A systematic method to predict and optimize oxidation resistance based on processing parameters, microstructural features, and kinetic profiles is still lacking. Despite extensive experimental evidence, the ability to forecast, in advance, which combinations of process modifications (or alloy compositions) will yield the best protective oxide layers under given environmental conditions remains an open challenge.
decision.lever: Develop an integrated data-driven model that assimilates experimental datasets (e.g., oxidation kinetics, microstructural metrics, and compositional information) to predict the formation of protective oxide scales and oxidation resistance performance.
decision.why: This approach follows the trend of accumulating high-quality experimental data on oxidation behavior. By leveraging machine learning, researchers can build predictive models that not only capture the complex relationships observed in prior experiments but also guide optimization of processing parameters, thereby addressing the unsolved challenge of reliably forecasting oxidation resistance in susceptible metallic surfaces.
